title: Tidal Announces Ban on AI-Generated Music Starting December 9, with Over 29 Million Songs Expected to Be Taken Down by Year-End

content_html:
Music streaming platform Tidal has announced that starting December 9, it will ban and remove music entirely generated by artificial intelligence, with more than 29 million songs expected to be removed from the platform by the end of 2026. Once the new rules take effect, Tidal expects to reject about 80,000 to 85,000 song upload requests per day. It will also prohibit distribution services from submitting tracks that are 100% AI-generated, and will refuse to include songs whose metadata explicitly marks them as entirely AI-made.

Tidal said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of the songs it received were detected as AI-generated. The platform currently has 27 million fully AI-generated songs, accounting for 6.3% of its total catalog, but 96% of them have no plays. Tidal believes that a large amount of AI-generated content is crowding out the visibility of original music, making it harder for users to discover real artists and original works.

This policy further tightens Tidal's previous AI music management measures. In June this year, the platform had already removed monetization eligibility for fully AI-made songs, but Robert Anderson, head of Tidal Music, said the measure did not create enough of a deterrent. The new rules still leave room for AI-assisted creation: music that uses AI tools for part of the creative process but is not entirely AI-generated can still be uploaded.

As AI-generated music floods streaming platforms, industry regulatory strategies are diverging. Following Bandcamp, Tidal has become another mainstream platform to adopt a full ban; Deezer offers AI music detection tools and plans to launch content filtering, while Spotify and YouTube Music mainly identify AI-generated content through labels.

On the other hand, record labels are exploring partnerships with streaming platforms and AI model developers to expand revenue through music licensing, model training, and remix features. Goldman Sachs predicts that by 2035, AI-related licensing tools and new revenue models could boost record labels' revenue by 10%. Tidal's adjustment also reflects the balancing pressure streaming platforms face among AI content governance, original music protection, and commercial interests.
